newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economist - dlr may rise more against mark.
newsitem.headline: German economist - dlr may rise more against mark.

text.p: The U.S. dollar has potential for the time being to appreciate further against the mark but in the longer term the U.S. unit will be dampened as German economic growth picks up, a senior German economist said on Monday.

Hermann Remsperger, chief economist of BHF-Bank AG, said the dollar could gain ground because the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates to counter the threat of inflation as U.S. wages, capacity utilisation and consumer spending are rising.

"Economic and interest rate considerations for the time being provide the dollar with upward potential against the mark," Remsperger said in the text of a speech to be held at a conference on currency issues here.
Remsperger also said the prospect of European monetary union would continue to unsettle currency markets in coming months.

"In the longer term the U.S. lead on interest rates and economic growth is likely to shrink. That will dampen the dollar in the long term. Political statements on exchange rates are unlikely to change these trends fundamentally."
Remsperger was speaking after economic policymakers from the Group of Seven issued what dealers regarded as a benign statement on currencies after their meeting in Washington on Sunday.
The G7 said major foreign exchange misalignments had been corrected, that excessive volatility was undesirable and that there was a need to avoid currency moves that could lead to unbalanced trade.

But the statement did not make any explicit reference to dollar strength or yen weakness, nor did it suggest that active intervention from German, Japanese or U.S. central banks was imminent, traders and analysts said.
Currency traders reacted by pushing the dollar to a three-year high against the mark of 1.7389, and above 127 yen, just shy of a four-and-a-half year peak of 127.19 touched earlier this month.
Remsperger predicted that the Fed's credit tightening policy could weaken U.S. economic growth in 1998 to two percent from a projected three percent in 1997.
He predicted yields on U.S. 10-year bonds will rise to about 7.5 percent in the next six months. Yields should fall slightly in the following six months, he added.
The German economy was in a cyclical uptrend hampered by structural factors like labour market problems, high taxes and difficulties in the construction sector, Remsperger said.
He predicted German gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by 2.5 percent in 1997 and by 2.5 to three percent in 1998.

"With this growth prospect the forward-looking Bundesbank could towards end-1997 face the question of switching to a less relaxed monetary policy despite continued pleasingly low inflation," Remsperger said.
He added he could also imagine that nations participating in the planned single currency may agree on a co-ordinated rise in interest rates after the choice of euro members is made in May 1998.

German bond yields will rise as economic growth gains pace and amid uncertainty concerning the euro, Remsperger said. He predicted 10-year yields on German government bond, or Bunds, will be about half to three quarters of a percentage point above current levels in one year's time. Bunds were yielding about 5.9 percent at 0820 GMT.
"The euro is likely to continue causing unrest on the currency markets in the coming months because there is constant change in favourites among the scenarios for monetary union," Remsperger said.
The scenarios are a punctual euro launch on January 1, 1999 with a limited number of members, a start with many members and the "political taboo" of a delay, Remsperger said.
"If the probability of a launch en masse increases, the dollar will gain wings," Remsperger said. "The prospect f a delay would appreciate the mark.
But a delay would only give the mark a temporary boost if Germany was in part responsible for the postponement, Remsperger added.
Independent economists have cast doubt over Germany's ability to qualify in time for the euro and say this could lead to a delay of the project.
--David Crossland, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
